## Overview

The Sandawe are an indigenous ethnic group of Southeast Africa based in the Chemba District kwamtoro ward of Dodoma Region in central Tanzania. Their population was estimated at 40,000 in 2000, while the Sandawe language article describes about 60,000 Sandawe people in Dodoma Region. Sandawe is a tonal language with click consonants and is unrelated to neighbouring Bantu languages, though it has been influenced by neighbouring Cushitic languages. The Sandawe are associated with hunting, gathering, agriculture, herding, oral tradition, singing, dancing, music, ritual, and storytelling. Their culture is described as insular and deeply spiritual, with animism, ancestor relations, and respect for spirits connected to caves in the hills.

## Material culture

### Architecture

The Sandawe built very temporary huts away from water holes. Their homesteads were scattered wherever suitable land was found for staple crops, and they were uncomfortable with denser village life.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 They mention hoes in connection with cooperative hoeing, and cattle in the context of colonial-era conflict.

## Music & performance

The Sandawe are described as fond of singing, dancing, making music, and drinking beer, and as possessing an enormous store of songs. Ceremonials and rituals differed from one another, including harvest and courtship ceremonies, curing rituals involving trances, circumcision festivals, and *simba* possession dances. In *simba* dances, dancers imitated lions in order to combat witchcraft.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name *simba* possession dances, in which dancers imitated lions to combat witchcraft. They also describe dancing as part of Sandawe ceremonial and ritual life, including harvest, courtship, curing, and circumcision contexts.

## Festivals & rituals

The Sandawe performed rituals of sacrifice once a year at caves in the hills, which were believed to harbour spirits. The caves were respected and feared: animals were not herded there, and wood was not cut or twigs broken. People went to the caves as a group, shouting prayers to assure the spirits that they had come to pay their respects rather than disturb them. These prayers were shouted as loudly as possible so that the spirits could hear them.

Sandawe ceremonial life also included harvest and courtship ceremonies, curing rituals with trances, circumcision festivals, and *simba* possession dances. The moon was regarded as a symbol of life and fertility; it brought rain and controlled the cycle of fertility in women. The mantis was considered a divine messenger, and a medium was usually consulted to explain its appearance.

## Foodways

The Sandawe adopted agriculture from their Bantu neighbours, probably the Gogo. Their staple crops were millet, sorghum, and eventually maize. They also had a strong hunting and gathering tradition and were regarded as expert survivalists during food shortages. Informal parties were organised to hunt pigs and elephants. By the late 1880s to early 1890s, they had also become herders and agriculturalists.

The sources mention drinking beer.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Sandawe retain a strong oral tradition and enjoy recounting stories that embody the collective wisdom of the group. In telling their stories, they identify with small animals that use cunning and intelligence to outwit dangerous and more powerful enemies.

## Language & religion

Sandawe is spoken in the Dodoma Region of Tanzania and has two dialects, northwest and southeast. Differences include speaking speed, vowel dropping, word taboo, and minor lexical and grammatical differences. Language use is vigorous among adults and children, and some areas are monolingual. Sandawe has five vowel qualities, click consonants, and a tonal system; the language article describes seven phonetic tones.

The language has been classified historically in relation to the defunct Khoisan family, while the Khoe languages are presented as its most promising relative. Sandawe religion is described as animist and centred on spirits, ancestors, the moon, stars, seasons, and the mantis. Warongwe was regarded as a distant and abstract god who was rarely prayed to or given sacrifices.
